O R D E R
Before the Court took up the main matter, Mr. Rajdeep Rastogi,
learned Senior Counsel, as an Officer of the Court, brought to its
notice that coaching centers were operating from Commercial areas
and were required to be relocated to the areas earmarked for

--- Page 30 ---
11
M.A. (C) D. No. 17103/2026
coaching institutes, which had been demarcated by the Government /
Jaipur Development Authority itself. Pursuant thereto, and upon the
matter being brought to the notice of the Court, the Authorities,
particularly the Jaipur Development Authority, had issued notices
to such coaching institutes to shift to the designated areas.
2. However, Mr. Rajdeep Rastogi, learned Senior Counsel, who is
present in Court, submits that while returning, he received four
missed calls, which he did not answer. The Secretary of the Welfare
Society, who was also travelling with Mr. Rajdeep Rastogi, learned
Senior Counsel, answered the phone, whereupon the caller threatened
him with dire consequences. The matter was reported to the police
and  an FIR was registered on 12.09.2026. However, till date,
nothing substantial appears to have been done. If that be the
position, we take serious note of the same. An Officer of the Court
or, for that matter, any person who assists the Court, must be able
to discharge his duties without fear or apprehension. It is the
duty of the Court to ensure that no harm comes to such person, and
the Court would leave no stone unturned to protect such persons.
3. Accordingly, the Chief Secretary, State of Rajasthan, as well
as  the  Director  General  of  Police,  Rajasthan,  shall  appear
personally before this Court the day after tomorrow, when the
matter shall be taken up in the post-lunch session, to apprise the
Court of the up-to-date status and also to explain why there has
been such slackness on the part of the Authorities concerned.
4. Mr. Ajit Kumar Sinha, learned amicus curiae , points out that
in terms of the previous order of the Court, local site inspections

--- Page 31 ---
12
M.A. (C) D. No. 17103/2026
have been carried out in Delhi and Lucknow, in respect whereof a
status report has been filed by him. Learned counsel appearing for
IIT Delhi informs the Court that a report has also been filed
pursuant to the inspection conducted. The same are taken on record.
However, Mr. Ajit Kumar Sinha, learned amicus curiae , submits that
the role of the New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) has not been
cooperative, inasmuch as neither any assistance was provided nor
was any responsible Officer present during the inspection.
5. At this juncture, Mr. K.M. Nataraj, learned ASG, submits that
he shall ensure full cooperation on behalf of the NDMC in all
respects and that there shall be no complaint from the learned
amicus  curiae  in future. We are confident that the learned ASG
would sensitise the NDMC, particularly its Commissioner, with
regard to the seriousness of the matter and the strict view that
the Court would take if there is even the slightest attempt not to
cooperate.
6. By the next date, the entire exercise shall be completed and
the learned amicus  curiae  is requested to submit a final report
confined to the areas indicated in the previous order.
7. In terms of the order of this Court, Mr. Animesh Parashar, the
then  Municipal  Commissioner,  Patna  Municipal  Corporation  and
presently  holding  the  post  of  Bihar  Urban  Infrastructure
Development Corporation (BUDCO), has appeared in person and filed
his  reply  to  the  show  cause  notice.  He  has  tendered  an
unconditional and unqualified apology.
8. Having regard to the aforesaid, his personal appearance is

--- Page 32 ---
13
M.A. (C) D. No. 17103/2026
dispensed with, for the present.
9. Mr.  Gopal Sankaranarayanan, learned Senior Counsel, submits
that he has filed I.A. No. 277011/2026 and I.A. No. 290689/2026
with regard to the grievance of persons who neither fall within the
category of unauthorised construction nor that of unauthorised use
of the premises in question in Jaipur and Bhopal.
10. Let a copy of the same be served upon the learned  amicus
curiae as also upon the concerned Authority, as may be relevant for
the said purpose. The learned amicus  curiae  is requested to look
into the same and seek instructions from the Authorities.
11. Let a copy thereof be served by learned Senior Counsel upon
learned counsel appearing for the States of Madhya Pradesh and
Rajasthan.
12. As a large number of petitions have been filed by various
parties, we request the respective parties to serve a copy thereof
upon the learned amicus curiae as well as upon the learned counsel
appearing for the concerned States. The learned amicus curiae shall
file a report in respect thereof after obtaining instructions from
the Authorities, and the Authorities are also directed to file a
detailed  response  thereto.  It  is  made  clear  that  all
Authorities/persons, whether private or official, shall extend full
cooperation to the learned  amicus  curiae  with regard to whatever
information is sought or whatever assistance is required by him.
13. Mr. S.D. Sanjay, learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of
the MCD, submits that the MCD has filed its compliance report. The
same is taken on record.

--- Page 33 ---
14
M.A. (C) D. No. 17103/2026
14. Mr. K.M. Nataraj, learned ASG, has filed the SIT report in a
sealed cover. The same is taken on record.
15. Ms. Kavitha Rameshwar Nithyanandam, learned AAG for the State
of Tamil Nadu, submits that the proceedings pending before the
regional authorities have been taken up on priority and five more
Officers have been assigned for the purpose. It is submitted that
almost 260 cases have been disposed of and the remaining cases are
also likely to be disposed of within a few months. Having regard to
the aforesaid, time is extended to the Authorities to complete the
exercise by 07.11.2026.
16. Learned amicus curiae points out that the State of Uttarakhand
has neither entered appearance nor deposited a sum of Rs. 50,000/-
(Rupees Fifty Thousand), nor filed an affidavit in the proceedings
till date. We take serious objection to such conduct. Accordingly,
notice of contempt is issued against the Chief Secretary, State of
Uttarakhand. He shall remain present before the Court on the next
date of listing.
17. Mr. K.M. Nataraj, learned ASG appearing for the State of
Madhya Pradesh, submits that by order dated 05.08.2026, this Court
had stayed the resolution of the State Government appointing a
Committee to examine certain issues relating to the Master Plan for
the  city  of  Bhopal  and  to  submit  a  report.  However,  upon
reconsideration, the Government has taken a decision to withdraw
the said resolution and the proposal for constitution of the
Committee. 
18. We note the same and expect that the same shall be done within

--- Page 34 ---
15
M.A. (C) D. No. 17103/2026
one week.
19. For the present, the Authorities shall give priority to
ensuring that no commercial activity takes place in areas earmarked
exclusively for residential use.
20. Accordingly, the following directions are issued:
(i) For the present, the Authorities shall give priority to
ensuring that in areas specifically shown as residential, where the
permission granted by the State Government is only for residential
use, no commercial activity takes place. If any commercial activity
is found to be taking place in such areas, the premises shall, in
the first instance, be sealed. 
(ii)  In  areas  which  are  not  clearly  specified  for  any
particular use, such as commercial or residential use, the question
of mixed use may also require consideration. However, for the time
being, the status quo shall not be disturbed. Proceedings on paper
may nevertheless continue. 
(iii) With regard to any building/land/area in respect of
which a  lis may be pending, whether between private individuals
concerning title or any other dispute, or between the Government
and the concerned party, the pendency of such lis shall not come in
the way of the Authorities sealing the premises if the use thereof
is in violation of the purpose for which the land/building was
allotted and for which the Competent Authority has sanctioned and
approved the plan. 
21. It is clarified that if it is found that any structure has
come up wholly unauthorised and without any approval whatsoever

--- Page 35 ---
16
M.A. (C) D. No. 17103/2026
from any Authority, much less from the Competent Authority, the
process of sealing/demolition, as may be required in accordance
with law, shall also proceed.
22. We make it clear that all Authorities required to act in terms
of the orders passed by this Court in the present proceedings shall
carry out the exercise without any discrimination. If it is brought
to the notice of the Court that the Authorities have resorted to
any pick-and-choose approach, this Court shall take a strict view
of the matter.
23. In some places, particularly Bhopal, the learned amicus curiae
informs the Court that he has received information that on the one
hand, the orders of this Court are not being fully complied with,
while, on the other hand, they are also being selectively misused
inasmuch as a building/complex/property is initially sealed but is
thereafter unsealed within a few hours or days, without any
intervening development, such as submission of a show-cause reply
or a decision having been taken by the Authority.
24. At this juncture, Mr. K.M. Nataraj, learned ASG, submits that
there may have been some confusion on account of the Government
having constituting a Committee, which shall now be withdrawn and
that the aforesaid issue may therefore no longer arise. 
25. At this juncture, Mr. K.M. Nataraj, learned ASG, submits that
the Master Plan for Bhopal has not been revised since the year 1995
and that the Government has now prepared a draft Master Plan. It is
submitted that this Court may permit the same to be notified so
that objections may at least be invited and the process may

--- Page 36 ---
17
M.A. (C) D. No. 17103/2026
proceed. However, it is assured that without the permission of this
Court, the same shall not be finalized.
26. Having considered the same, we permit publication of the draft
State Master Plan. We clarify that the test to be applied by the
Authorities with regard to any property/construction shall be
whether the same is in conformity with the existing Master Plan and
the applicable building bye-laws of the Competent Authority.
27. After the order was dictated, learned counsel appearing for
the State of Rajasthan sought time to take telephonic instructions
from the Director General of Police, Rajasthan, on the issue. It is
assured that strict action shall be taken in the matter within 24
hours. In view of the aforesaid assurance, for the present, the
personal appearance of the Chief Secretary and the Director General
of Police, Rajasthan, is dispensed with.
28. The Court is conscious of the fact that the learned amicus
curiae has constituted a team for this work, which we realise is
time-consuming and taxing. Thus, by way of honorarium, let a cheque
for a sum of Rs. 10,00,000/- (Rupees Ten Lakhs) be issued in the
name of Mr. Ajit Kumar Sinha, learned  amicus  curiae , by the
Registry from out of the funds deposited by the States in the
present matter, to meet the secretarial expenses and also as a
token honorarium for the other members of the team.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.             OF 2026

STATE OF CHHATTISGARH                        RESPONDENT(S)
 O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. Briefly stated, the facts of the case are that on the
night of 09.08.2018, appellant’s wife and two children
were found dead with injuries in their home. Subsequently,
FIR No.217 dated 10.08.2018 came to be registered against
the appellant at Police Station Chakrabhata, District
Bilaspur, under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
(for short “IPC”). The appellant was taken into custody on
suspicion of the murders the next evening.
2.1   The  prosecution’s  case  rested  entirely  on
circumstantial evidence. The Trial Court in Sessions Case
No.144/2018,  relying  on  the  last-seen  theory,  the
appellant’s unexplained absence and recovery of the weapon
1

--- Page 57 ---
and clothes, held that the appellant, driven by financial
difficulties, had murdered his wife and two children. The
Trial Court convicted the appellant under Section 302 of
the IPC and sentenced him to life imprisonment  for each
of the three murders to run concurrently.
2.2   The appellant’s appeal, being CRA No.706 of 2021,
was dismissed by the High Court, which invoked Section 106
of  the  Indian  Evidence  Act,  1872  to  hold  that  the
appellant had failed to explain the deaths occurring
within his own household and his absence at the relevant
time.
2.3   Aggrieved by the dismissal of his appeal, the
appellant has preferred the present appeal. 
3. We have heard learned counsel, Dr.  Nirmal Chopra for
the appellant and learned standing counsel and Deputy
Advocate General appearing for the respondent-State of
Chhattisgarh. We have perused the material on record.
4. During the course of submissions, learned counsel for
the appellant drew our attention to one crucial aspect of
the matter since we were not inclined to interfere with
the case on merits, that is, with regard to the nature of
2

--- Page 58 ---
the sentence imposed on the appellant by the Trial Court
vide its judgment dated 28.05.2021. Noting the gruesome
multiple murders that were committed by the appellant in a
single incident, the Trial Court observed as under:
“63. On the question of punishment, the accused,
his advocate and the Public Prosecutor on behalf
of  the  prosecution  were  heard.  The  accused
submitted that he is a first-time offender and
the act appears to have been committed due to
financial  difficulties,  hence  a  lenient  view
should be adopted.
64. This case does not appear to be of the
rarest category, it appears that the accused,
troubled  by  financial  difficulties,  committed
this act with the intention of not allowing his
family  to  suffer  before  committing  suicide.
Therefore, considering the entire circumstances
of the case, the accused Amjad Khan is punished
as follows:-

All  three  imprisonments  will  be  served
simultaneously. It is noteworthy that the accused
Amjad Khan has not only killed his wife but also
his two small innocent children, therefore in
this case life imprisonment will mean till the
death of the accused Amjad Khan.
65. In this case, the accused has been in
judicial custody for a total of 02 years, 09
months and 17 days from 11-08-2018 to today’s
date 28-05-2021, this period will be adjusted
with the period of imprisonment under Section 428
of  the  Code  of  Criminal  Procedure,  the
certificate is mentioned after the judgment.”
5. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the
Trial  Court  could  not  have  while  awarding  life
imprisonment also qualified the same by stating that the
life  imprisonment  will  mean  “till  the  death  of  the
accused”. Drawing our attention to Section 302 of the IPC,
he contended that the life imprisonment could not have
been qualified by the Trial Court; that it is only for a
constitutional Court such as the High Court or this Court
4

--- Page 60 ---
which could qualify a life sentence having regard to the
facts and circumstances of the case. Learned counsel
further submitted that the sentence imposed by the Trial
Court would also deprive the appellant from claiming
remission which is not only a constitutional right but
also  a  statutory  right.  Hence,  that  portion  of  the
judgment of the Trial Court imposing a life imprisonment
which would mean “till the death of the appellant” may be
modified and the imprisonment could be life imprisonment
simpliciter.
6. Per contra, learned Deputy Advocate General appearing
for the respondent-State supported the judgment of the
High Court which has sustained the judgment of the Trial
Court imposing such a sentence. He contended that although
the Trial Court may not have imposed such a sentence, when
the High Court has affirmed it, as a constitutional Court
such a sentence could be imposed by the High Court. He,
therefore, submitted that there is no merit in this
appeal.
7. We have considered the arguments advanced at the bar.
At the outset, we extract Section 302 of the IPC which
reads as under:
5

--- Page 61 ---
“302. Punishment for murder.— Whoever commits
murder  shall  be  punished  with  death,  or
imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable
to fine.”
8. The nature of punishment for an offence under Section
300 is life imprisonment and fine. The said sentence is
not qualified either in terms of the number of years or in
any other manner.  Life imprisonment which is imposed by
the Trial Court in the instant case is at the discretion
of the Trial Court as Section 302 also imposes a death
penalty. The Trial Court in the instant case has not
exercised its discretion to impose the death penalty but
on the other hand has imposed  life imprisonment and fine
as a sentence. However, the qualification of the “life
imprisonment” with “till death of the accused” is not
warranted in terms of the Section 302 of the IPC.
9. We find that with the passage of time, the High Court
as well as this Court while substituting a death penalty
with  sentence  of  life  imprisonment  has  exercised
discretion depending upon the facts and circumstances of
each case by qualifying the sentence of life imprisonment
to mean a certain number of years without remission. In
other words, instead of imposing death penalty, the High
6

--- Page 62 ---
Court or this Court directs that the accused-convict must
complete a certain number of years before he can seek
release. Such sentences are imposed by the constitutional
Courts such as the High Court or this Court. But in the
instant case, we find that the Trial Court has qualified
the sentence of life imprisonment to mean “till the death
of the accused”. As a result, the appellant-accused now
convict cannot have an opportunity to seek remission of
his sentence which is permissible both under Article 72 as
well as Article 163 of the Constitution of India as a
constitutional remedy by making an appropriate application
either before the President of India or the Governor of
the State respectively. Be that as it may,  such an
appellant here would also not have the statutory right to
seek remission by making an application under Section 432
read with relevant provisions of the Code of Criminal
Procedure, 1973. Therefore, according to learned counsel
for the appellant, the right of the appellant to seek
remission in the phase of a sentence of life imprisonment
has  been  totally  negated  by  holding  that  the  life
imprisonment would mean till the death of the accused. 
7

--- Page 63 ---
10. Learned counsel for the appellant also contended that
this aspect of the matter has not been noticed by the high
Court while affirming the judgment of conviction and
sentence. He, therefore, submitted that sentence imposed
by the Trial Court, namely, life imprisonment, till the
death of the accused, may be modified to mean life
imprisonment simpliciter. 
11. On the other hand, learned Deputy Advocate General
submitted that the affirmation of the said sentence would
mean that the constitutional Court, namely, the High Court
has taken note of the same and hence, the said sentence
need not be interfered with by this Court particularly
having regard to the multiple murders in the same incident
of the wife and two innocent children (daughter and son)
and gravity and seriousness of the offences.
12. In  Swamy Shraddananda (2) vs. State of Karnataka,
(2008) 13 SCC 767, a three-judge bench of this Court found
it necessary to make a special category for the very few
cases where the death penalty might be substituted by the
punishment of imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a
term in excess of fourteen years and to put that category
beyond the application of remission.
8

--- Page 64 ---
13. Thereafter, the Constitution Bench of this Court in
Union  of  India  vs.  V.  Sriharan,  (2016)  7  SCC  1
(“Sriharan”),  considered,  inter  alia,  the  question,
whether a special category of sentence instead of death
for a term exceeding fourteen years can be made by putting
that category beyond grant of remission?
14. This Court in Sukhdev Yadav @ Pehalwan vs. State of
(NCT of Delhi) & Others  ,    (2025) 7 S.C.R. 2012  , while
considering the question of whether a convict who has
completed his life imprisonment for a fixed term of
sentence without remission, is entitled to be released
from prison on completion of such a sentence. While
considering  the  same,  one  of  us  (Nagarathna,  J.)
interpreted the decision of  Sriharan in the following
terms:  
“10.6After referring in detail to the judgement
of  Swamy Shraddananda 2 , it was observed that
when by way of a judicial decision, after a
detailed  analysis,  having  regard  to  the
proportionality of the crime committed, it is
decided that the offender deserves to be punished
with the sentence of life imprisonment i.e. till
end of his life or for a specific period of
twenty years, thirty years or forty years, such a
conclusion  should  survive  without  any
interruption. In such an event, it can be stated
that  such  punishment  imposed  will  have  no
remission or other such liberal approach should
not come into effect to nullify such imposition.
9

--- Page 65 ---
Accepting the submission of learned Solicitor
General that there is no restriction to fix any
period beyond fourteen years and up to the end of
one’s life span, it was stated that the Court can
sentence the accused to undergo imprisonment for
a specified period even beyond fourteen years
without any scope for remission. The Court can
direct that such offender is not to be released
early and be kept in confinement for a longer
period by imposition of an appropriate sentence”.
10.7 Moving further it was observed that nowhere
under the IPC is there any prohibition that the
imprisonment cannot be imposed for any specific
period  within  the  lifespan.  Thus,  when  life
imprisonment is imposed, the Court can specify
the period up to which the said sentence of life
should remain, befitting the nature of the crime
committed, when the Court’s conscience does not
persuade the death penalty. Therefore, the dictum
in Swamy Shraddananda (2) was approved by this
Court by observing that within the prescribed
limit of life imprisonment, imprisonment for a
specified  period  would  be  a  proportionate
punishment having regard to the nature of the
crime as well as the interest of the victim.
10.8 Therefore, the law-makers have thought it
fit to prescribe the minimum and maximum sentence
to be imposed having regard to the nature of
crime and have left it to the Courts to determine
the kind of punishments that have to be imposed
within the prescribed limit under the relevant
provision. In other words, while the maximum
extent of punishment of either death or life
imprisonment is provided for under the relevant
provisions, it will be for the Courts to decide
if, in its opinion, the imposition of death may
not be warranted, what should be the number of
years of imprisonment that would be judiciously
and  judicially  more  appropriate.  This  is  by
taking into account, apart from the crime itself,
the interest of the society at large and other
relevant factors which cannot be put in any
straight jacket formula. The said process of
10

--- Page 66 ---
determination must be held to be available with
the courts by virtue of extent of the punishments
provided for such specified nature of crimes and
such power is also to be derived from those penal
provisions themselves.”
15. Sriharan itself  concluded  on  this  point  in  the
following terms: 
“105.We, therefore, reiterate that the power
derived from the Penal Code for any modified
punishment within the punishment provided for in
the Penal Code for such specified offences can
only be exercised by the High Court and in the
event of further appeal only by the Supreme Court
and not by any other court in this country. To
put  it  differently,  the  power  to  impose  a
modified punishment providing for any specific
term of incarceration or till the end of the
convict’s life as an alternate to death penalty,
can be exercised only by the High Court and the
Supreme Court and not by any other inferior
court.”
16. This position was reaffirmed in Shiva Kumar vs. State
of Karnataka, (2023) 9 SCC 817 (“Shiva Kumar”) , wherein
this  Court  clarified  that  the  observations  of  the
Constitution Bench in Sriharan could not be read narrowly.
Oka, J. held as under: 
“14. Hence, we have no manner of doubt that even
in a case where capital punishment is not imposed
or is not proposed, the constitutional courts can
always exercise the power of imposing a modified
or fixed-term sentence by directing that a life
sentence,  as  contemplated  by  “secondly”  in
Section 53 IPC, shall be of a fixed period of
more than fourteen years, for example, of twenty
11

--- Page 67 ---
years,  thirty  years  and  so  on.  The  fixed
punishment cannot be for a period less than 14
years in view of the mandate of Section 433-A
CrPC.”
17. Applying this principle, this Court in Shiva Kumar,
modified the sentence imposed by the Fast Track Court
(Sessions Court) on the appellant therein to undergo
rigorous imprisonment for rest of his life for an offence
punishable under Section 302 of the IPC to undergo thirty
years of actual sentence and to be released thereafter.
The appeal was partly allowed to the above extent.
18. The limits of this power were subsequently considered
in  Kiran vs. the State of Karnataka, (2025) 12 S.C.R.
1069, wherein this Court considered the issue whether, the
Sessions Court was competent to award a sentence of
imprisonment for life till the remainder of life. There,
the  accused  had  set  the  deceased  ablaze  by  pouring
kerosene over her, as a result of which, the deceased
sustained burns and succumbed to the same ten days later.
The Trial Court convicted the accused and sentenced him to
life imprisonment operating till the end of his natural
life. This Court, by order dated 08.11.2024, issued notice
limited to the question of whether the Trial Court was
12

--- Page 68 ---
correct in imposing the lifetime imprisonment on those
terms. Answering in the negative K. Vinod Chandran, J.
held as under:
“9. The sentence of life imprisonment no doubt
means  the  entire  life,  subject  only  to  the
remission and commutation provided under Cr. PC
and  also  to  Articles  72  and  161  of  the
Constitution of India, which cannot be curtailed
by a Sessions Court. Nor can the Sessions Court,
a creation of the Cr. PC curtail the provision
under Section 428, Cr. PC, available in the Code
which created it.
xxx
15. Going by the decisions cited, it has to be
held that life imprisonment awarded would be for
the  rest  of  the  life,  the  power  to  grant
remission and commutation under Sections 432 to
435 Cr. PC cannot be curtailed by the Sessions
Court, when the remission as provided under the
Constitution was declared to be not permissible
of interference by the Constitutional Courts. The
power of alternate sentencing to cover the hiatus
between 14 years and death, cannot be applied by
the Sessions Courts. Hence, the sentence of life
imprisonment cannot be directed to be till the
end of natural life, by the Sessions Court which
direction  would  be  in  conflict  with  the
provisions of the Cr. PC. The power of remission
or commutation conferred on the State cannot be
taken away and the sentence as awarded by the
trial court and confirmed by the High Court for
the offence under Section 302 of the Indian Penal
Code,  1860  is  confirmed  as  imprisonment  for
life.”
19. We have perused the judgment of the High Court in
light of aforesaid dicta and we find that there has been
13

--- Page 69 ---
no discussion on the nature of the sentence imposed by the
Trial Court on the appellant herein.
20. In the circumstances, we find that having regard to
the gravity of the offences alleged against the appellant
herein, we modify the sentence imposed on the appellant
from life imprisonment to mean “till the death of the
accused” to “life imprisonment, that is to say, twenty
years without any remission”.
21. The appeal is allowed in part in the aforesaid terms.
22. Consequently, the impugned judgment of the High Court
as well as judgment of the Trial Court stand modified to
the aforesaid extent only.
23. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.                            OF 2026
(@SLP(CRL.) Nos.1606-1607 OF 2026)
P. JEYAPANDIAN & ANR. ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
N. JOHN ISSAC & ANR.  ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Interim orders dated 05.12.2025 and 16.12.2025 passed by the High Court of
Madras at Madurai Bench in WPCRL(MD) No. 2391 of 2025  are under challenge.
4. The saga of this litigation dates back to 1945, namely, a suit OS No.15/1945
was filed for various reliefs which ultimately culminated in a decree being drawn
under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC) on 30.03.1946. As
per the said decree, six managers, three from Hindu Panikkars and three from
Christian Panikkars were empowered to manage the property of the Trust and
income flowing therefrom. It was also explicitly made clear in the said decree
1

--- Page 73 ---
that term of office of such managers would be five years and outgoing
managers would conduct elections for incoming managers and handover the
charge  to  them.  Originally  the  trust  was  named  as  “ Virudhunagar,
Thirumangalam,  Palayampatti,  KovilanKulam,  Periyakarisalkulam  Hindu,
Christian Panikar Community Trust ”. This was changed vide order dated
11.01.2017, which was also challenged in OS No.20/2012 and same came to be
dismissed  and  the  changed  name  of  the  trust  was  “ Virudhunagar,
Thirumangalam, Palayampatti, KovilanKulam, Periyakarisalkulam five villages of
Sriman Narayana Madam , Panikar Community of Paripalana Manging Trust ”.
The tenure of the last trustees, namely, the appellants herein, ended in August,
2021 and on account of fresh elections not having been conducted, the dispute
arose. It is stated that R Bhagavath Sing  and P Saravanan, Members of the
Hindu and Christian Panikars Community, have filed a suit in O.S. No.49/2023
against the trustees, including the appellants herein, seeking for a direction to
the defendants therein to convene a General Body Meeting to elect new
administrators to manage the property of the Trust and to appoint a Court
Commissioner to facilitate the process of election. Written statements are said
to have been filed and the suit is said to be pending. Be that as it may.
5. On account of there being a possibility of the peace and tranquility being
disturbed, the jurisdictional Tahsildar of Virudhunagar conducted a peace
meeting on 17.12.2025 wherein the parties are said to have agreed upon to
abide by the orders that may be said to have been passed in OS No.49/2023.
2

--- Page 74 ---
On account of wall posters and templates being circulated and demonstration
having been conducted by a particular group, the Deputy Superintendent of
Police, Virudhunagar, issued summons to the trustees, including the present
appellants, whereunder the parties were directed to workout the modalities as
per the outcome of the pending suit. It is at that juncture, the Respondent No.1
herein, is said to have submitted a representation to Superintendent of Police
seeking police protection during the General Body Meeting which was scheduled
to be held on 07.12.2025. A writ petition, namely, WPCRL(MD) No. 2391 of 2025
(Supra) came to be filed by Respondent No.1 herein seeking for a Writ of
Mandamus before the Superintendent of Police to consider the representation
dated 26.11.2025 to give necessary protection for the General Body Meeting
scheduled to be held on 07.12.2025. In fact, there is no mention or reference in
the writ petition about the pendency of the suit OS No. 49/2023. Appellants
herein also filed an Interlocutory Application to get impleaded as party-
respondents in the said writ petition and same is said to have been allowed. In
the said writ petition, the impugned order has been passed on 05.12.2025 by
appointing an Election Commissioner and ordering for election to be conducted
to the Trust in accordance with the decree dated 30.03.1946 passed in OS No.
15/1945 and further order came to be passed on 16.12.2025 by issuing certain
directions. Hence, these appeals.
6. Having heard the learned advocates appearing for the parties and on perusal
of the case papers, it would not detain us too long to set the dispute to a
3

--- Page 75 ---
quietus. A Perusal of the decree that came to be passed in scheme suit would
clearly indicate that first Committee of Mangers would hold the office for a
period of five years and fresh elections would be held once in five years and the
future  elections  shall  be  held  by  the  outgoing  Committee  of  Managers
themselves.  In paragraph 9 of the said decree, it is clearly and explicitly
indicated as under :
“9. The first committee of managers shall hold office for a
period of 5 years, and fresh elections shall be held once in 5
years. The future elections shall be held by the out going
committee of managers themselves. If within the period of 5
years, any membes cause to be one by reason of death or
any other cause, such vacancy shall be filed up in a meeting
of the community held as a whole. The list now prepared by
the commissioner shall be revised and additions made once
in every 5 years and before the election of committee of
managers  for  that  period  by  deleting  the  non-existing
panikkar member and adding the panikkar member who has
attained majority in the meanwhile.”
7. The present dispute seems to have arisen in the year 2021 when the then
existing Committee of Managers, who completed five year tenure, not having
conducted the election. The decree aforesaid is a complete answer to all the
questions raised not only in these appeals but also to all the disputes. We say
so for the simple reason that even the parties to the scheme suit, which
resulted in decree to be passed in wayback in the year 1946, were ad idem or
as to how to workout the future disputes. It was agreed upon by them that if
there were to be any difficulty in working out the scheme, any member of the
community (Whether Christian or Hindu) was entitled to apply to the Court for
suitable directions. The clause 14 as agreed upon between the parties reads as
under:
4

--- Page 76 ---
“14. If any alteration, variation or change in respect of this
scheme is found necessary and if any difficulty is felt in
working out this scheme, any member of the community
(Whether christian or Hindu) may apply to this court for
suitable directions. This court after notice to the parties on
record shall after hearing the objections, pass suitable orders
thereon. The application shall be made in this suit itself.”
8.  It  is  for  this  reason,  we  are  perforced  to  observe  as  to  the  very
maintainability of the Suit in OS. No.49/2023. However, we refrain from
expressing any opinion in that regard, since the parties to the suit are not
before this Court. As noticed hereinabove and at the cost of the repetition, it is
noted that remedies to the parties for redressal of their grievance would lie
before the competent civil court, which has drawn a decree under Section 92 of
CPC.
9. Though Mr. M.S. Ganesh, learned senior counsel appearing for the appellants,
has made a valiant attempt to contend that the provisions 0f the Hindu
Religious Endowments Act would be attracted, which at first blush, looks
attractive, by deeper examination of the relevant provisions of the Act, we
notice that said contention cannot be accepted. Section 3 of the said Act is
complete answer to the said proposition and the said act being applicable only
to the Hindu Religious and Charitable Trust and the instant trust being a
combination of both Hindu and Christians, the provisions of the said Act would
not be applicable. Even otherwise, the decree that has been drawn under
Section 92 CPC would prevail and govern the parties and it is for this precise
5

--- Page 77 ---
reason we have observed hereinabove that parties would be at liberty to move
the jurisdictional court, Virudhunagar, for appropriate relief including the
direction for conducting an election, if necessary, by appointing a suitable
person.
10. Hence, we permit the parties or any Member of the community to approach
the competent civil court which administers the scheme suits as contemplated
under section 92 CPC to seek such remedy as may be available to them and
reserve liberty in that regard. At the same time, a person who has been
appointed as a Manager much earlier and their term having been ended in the
year 2021, would not be entitled to continue in administration of the Trust.
There are various allegations and counter allegations made with regard to mal-
administration, mismanagement etc. It is not for this Court or the Courts
exercising the power under Article 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India to
examine such disputed questions of fact. It is also an issue which will have to be
thrashed out before the civil court, if necessary, by evaluating the evidence that
may be tendered by the parties in the scheme suit. At the same time, the
decree which has been drawn in the scheme suit, requires to be effectively
implemented for the betterment of the community at large. Any infraction or
deviation would defeat the very purpose of creation of such Trust and the
decree drawn.
11. Hence, we deem it proper and appropriate to appoint a Receiver to
6

--- Page 78 ---
administer, manage and preserve the Trust and its properties until and unless a
duly constituted body is elected under the supervision of the jurisdictional civil court.
Hence, we hereby appoint Justice Ananthi, Former Judge, Madras High Court, as a
Receiver  of  Virudhunagar,  Thirumangalam,  Palayampatti,  KovilanKulam,
Periyakarisalkulam five villages of Sriman Narayana Madam, Panikar Community of
Paripalana  Manging  Trust and the existing trustees who are now managing the
properties of the trust, shall forthwith handover the charge and the Receiver shall
take charge and administer the trust in the manner he/she deems fit and the
receiver would be at liberty to seek such orders or directions as deemed fit for the
proper administration of the Trust from the jurisdictional civil court which has passed
the decree in OS No.15/1945 and the jurisdictional court shall fix the remuneration
of the receiver which shall be not less than Rs.1.50 lakhs per month.
12. In the light of the aforestated order, the impugned order which directs the
appointment of an Election Commissioner and the order dated 16.12.2025,
issuing directions would not be sustainable and it is hereby set aside.
Accordingly, the appeals stand disposed of. No order as to costs.
13. In the light of the aforesaid observations, the jurisdictional High Court shall
pass appropriate orders for consigning the writ petition(s) to records.

--- Page 79 ---
14. All pending application(s) stands consigned to records.

1
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CIVIL APPEAL  No..............D.No..53205 OF 2024
PRIYANKA SAXENA                               … APPELLANT
Versus
UNION OF INDIA & ORS.                             … RESPONDENTS
O  R  D  E  R
1. Delay condoned.
2. The appellant joined the Indian Air Force (for short `IAF’)  at the Air
Force Academy, Hyderabad in January 2002 and after her commissioning on 20th
December,  2003,  she  joined  the  41  Wing,  Jaisalmer  as  her  first  posting.
Subsequently, she got married to late Wing Commander Harshit Sinha on 13.11.2006.
Even after her marriage, the appellant had continued her services in the Indian Air
Force, maintaining dedication and loyalty to her work. She also received the award
of Commendation by Air Officer Commanding-in-Chief, HQ WAC AF. The appellant
then  gave  birth  to  her  first  daughter,  Vanshika  Sinha,  on  22nd  May,  2012.
Subsequently, due to her family commitments and for the purpose of looking after
the child and supporting her husband, who was a fighter pilot, she expressed

--- Page 97 ---
2
unwillingness for further extension of service or permanent commission and left the
service  without  opting  for  any  extension  of  service.
On 15.06.2016, the appellant gave birth to her second daughter, Miss Vanisha Sinha.
The  appellant's  husband  was  posted  to  Srinagar,  where  he  was  the  Flight
Commander of the fighter squadron, 51 Squadron, "Sword Arms". Unfortunately, her
husband met with a tragic death due to MiG-21 Bison aircraft crash near Jaisalmer
Airfield on 24.12.2021.
3.  Subsequent to this, the appellant submitted a series of applications to
various officials of the IAF, and other authorities requesting that she be reinstated in
the IAF, considering the fact that she had already served 10 years as a Short Service
Commissioned Officer.  However, the request for reinstatement was not acceded to,
citing  various  policies  of  the  Government  of  India  and  instructions.
On 11.4.2022, the appellant was informed that her case for reinstatement has not
been  recommended  by  the  competent  authority  and,  therefore,  rejected.
4. The appellant filed Original Application No. 2157 of 2022 before the
Armed Forces Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi (for short, `the Tribunal’) seeking
the following relief:
“(a) To call for records on the basis of which the Respondents have
not considered her case for grant of age relaxation to join the Indian
Air  Force  in  the  special  category  of  Veer  Nari  by  taking  into
consideration  her  past  10  years  of  SSC  service  which  she  has
rendered  as  Logistics  Branch  Officer  by  either  granting  her  re-
commission/reinstatement or even extending the method by treating
her as a fresh case of appointment to bring her case within the policy
framework with further order of grant of benefit of Past Service for the
purpose of rank, seniority, pay protection and other benefits as well as
rejected her case In terms of impugned  orders dated 02.02.2022,
07.02.2022 and 11.04.2022, and thereafter quash the same.

--- Page 98 ---
3
(b) Direct the respondents to induct the applicant as an officer in the
Indian Air Force with all consequential benefits by either granting her
re-commission/reinstatement or to bring her case within the policy
framework and treat her case as fresh case of appointment for the
purpose of induction only with further direction to extend the benefit
of past service of 10 years rendered by the applicant as SSC Officer
for the purpose of training, rank, seniority, pay protection and other
benefits.
(c) Pass such and other orders as this Hon'ble Tribunal may deem fit
and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case.”
5.  The appellant, relying upon her service profile from the time of her
commissioning in December 2003 until her release in December 2013, submitted that
she is seeking only a relaxation of the prescribed age criteria and reinstatement in
service. She contended that, having regard to her status as a widow of a defence
personnel who had herself previously served in the Armed Forces, she ought to be
granted an additional relaxation in the prescribed age limit so as to enable her to
seek re-entry into the Armed Forces. The appellant further contended that several
similarly situated persons had been granted such relaxation and emphasized that,
with the increasing induction of women into the Armed Forces, it was incumbent
upon the Government of India to take cognizance of this emerging category and
suitably modify its policy to accommodate aspirants similarly situated to her. The
appellant submitted that the mere absence of an existing policy governing such
cases could not, by itself, constitute a justification for declining to examine her case.
She, therefore, prayed that the existing policy be reviewed and suitably modified to
make it inclusive of persons similarly situated to her, namely, women officers who
had previously served in the Armed Forces and had subsequently become widows
of defence personnel.

--- Page 99 ---
4
6. The respondents opposed the prayer of the appellant and contended
that she had given up on her claim for continuation or permanent commission in
2013 and, therefore, her rights ceased to exist and she has no fundamental right to
seek reinstatement or re-employment.  The respondents contended that there is an
eligibility criteria which has been fixed at a maximum of 35 years by policy letter
dated 30.11.2017, and since the appellant has crossed that age of 35, her case
cannot be considered and relaxation cannot be granted to her,  and that, at best,
they can only provide assistance for seeking alternate employment through the
placement cell of the Indian Air Force.                                               
7. The Tribunal took note of the issue as to whether the services need to
have  appropriate  policy  to  facilitate  the  return  of  women  officers,  who  are
unfortunately widowed, placed in a compelling situation, and seeking re-entry into
the  services,  when  in  the  first  place  they  may  not  have  been  found  fit  for
extension/grant  of  permanent  commission.                              
8.  The Tribunal took note of the policy of 30.11.2017, which was essentially
to provide an opportunity to the family of a service personnel, who dies in harness,
to have another breadwinner who is willing to serve the armed forces and, therefore,
are  given  relaxation  in  age  for  entry  into  pre-commission  training.
It also considered that the selection for extension/permanent commission apart, the
fact remains that such officers who are released at 10/14 years are a trained pool of
officers who can still contribute to the organisation, if given an opportunity to re-
enter the services and also, it is an opportunity to rehabilitate our "Veer Naris".  The
Tribunal took note of the fact that this class of women officers do not have a policy
under which they can seek consideration for re-entry into the services. The Tribunal,
therefore, felt that the Government need to review the policy letter dated 30.11.2017
to make it inclusive for this class of women officers and also, that the Union could

--- Page 100 ---
5
also review the mode of induction in such cases and examine whether a separate
pre-induction training would suffice in place of the regular pre-commission training
as being done. The Tribunal disposed of the application on 18.05.2023 with the
following directions: 
“(a) Examine the necessity of having a suitable policy for women
SSCOs who have since been released from service, and are widowed
when their spouses serving in the Armed Forces die in harness, and
they  wish  to  re-join  the  Services  due  to  the  compelling
circumstances.
(b) In the light of the above, review the policy letter dated 30.11.2017
as applicable.
(c) File a compliance report within three months of this order, giving
details of the decisions arrived at.
(d) The exercise as indicated in '(a)' above be undertaken within a
period of three months and in case the policy change accrues in
favour of such a category, the benefit thereof be extended to this
applicant.”
9. Thus, no effective relief was granted to the appellant herein and the OA was
closed with the above directions.  Subsequently, the appellant filed MA No. 2390 of
2024  with  MA  2391/2024  in  OA  No.  2157  of  2022,  seeking  compliance  of  the
directions.  However, the Union of India filed a short affidavit, in which it was pointed
out that a decision has been taken and the minutes were recorded as below:
''21. Chairman PPOC directed that as there is an existing policy on the
subject of induction of widows of Armed Forces personnel into the
Armed Forces, a separate policy is not needed on the subject”
10.  By its order dated  02.07.2024, the Tribunal rejected the prayer made by the
appellant.                                          

--- Page 101 ---
6
11.  The present Civil Appeal was filed before this Court, along with leave to
appeal under Section 31 of the Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007, as against the
impugned final judgment and orders dated 18.5.2023 and 02.07.2024 passed in OA
No.2157 of 2022 and MA No.2390/2024 with MA 2391/2024 in OA No.2157/2022 by the
Tribunal.
12.  This Court, vide order dated 09.12.2024, granted leave to appeal and
issued notice on the application seeking condonation of delay as well as on the
appeal. 
13.  In  the  subsequent  hearing  dated  23.07.2026,  the  respondents  were
directed to seek instructions.  The respondents contended that since the appellant
has been released from service at her own will and after completion of initial SSC
tenure, she cannot be reinstated under the ambit of the judgment in  Secretary,
Ministry of Defence  vs.  Babita Puniya and others , (2020) 7 SCC 469.  The only
compassionate relaxation permitted for widows of armed forces member is their age
eligibility criteria for pre-commissioning training. It was explained that the appellant
was also not covered under that criteria for joining.                             
14.  We have heard learned counsel, appearing on behalf of the appellant as
well as learned Additional Solicitor General of India, appearing on behalf of the
respondents and carefully perused the material placed on record.
15. We have taken note of the fact that the case of the appellant is a very
peculiar one and not covered by any of the policies in existence framed by the Union
of India. The contentions raised as far as the eligibility and the age relaxation of the
appellant are without considering the fact that the appellant has served in the armed
forces earlier as a Short Service Commissioned Officer, and in normal course ought
to have got the benefit of relaxation of age as provided by the Government, even for
a SSC officer in civil services.  The appellant's case is one of a widow of a fighter

--- Page 102 ---
7
pilot who was serving in the Indian Air Force and who lost his life in an aircraft
crash. The appellant is a war widow having two school-going minor daughters, and
her  case  deserves  to  be  considered  sympathetically.  The  respondents  have
formulated a Policy for war widows with a noble object for their rehabilitation by
giving them various concessions, including reservation of seats but  a class of such
war widows like the appellant have been left out completely.  It seems to us that the
appellant’s  past service ought to have been given weightage, and her experience of
service  need  not  even  require  her  to  undergo  a  fresh  training,  a  fresh  pre-
commission training, which is mandatory in case of other war widows who are
inducted based on their academic qualification.  This is a case of the appellant
becoming eligible on both counts; her being an ex-Air Force officer, and she being a
war widow of an Air Force officer.                                                
16. Considering the peculiarity of the facts of the present case, and the
circumstances  under  which  the  appellant  had  to  approach  the  Court  for
reinstatement, and exercising our powers under Article 142 of the Constitution of
India,  we direct that the case of the appellant be treated as a single case without
creating any precedent, and she be re-inducted and reinstated into the Air Force in
the following terms :
1. The appellant is to undergo refresher training for a period of one
year from next course, as applicable.
2. During the training, the appellant will be governed by the rules
and regulations as applicable to trainees.
3. The appellant is to undergo and clear the medical requirements
for re-instatement.
4. On completion of training, the appellant would be reinstated as
Squadron Leader in the eleventh year of service (counting her previous

--- Page 103 ---
8
service rendered).
5. The appellant shall continue to be a short service commissioned
officer and would be granted extension of four years as per policy.
6. The appellant’s  inter-se seniority will be fixed along with her
current  peer  group  only  and  she  shall  be  considered for  Permanent
Commission, promotion etc. in future as per policy applicable along with
her current peer group.
  
17.  Accordingly, we allow the present appeal with a direction that the
appellant shall be reinstated in the Indian Air Force, subject to the conditions
mentioned above.  The impugned orders of the Armed Forces Tribunal, Principal
Bench, New Delhi, dated 18.05.2023 and 02.07.2024 are hereby set aside.
18. It is clarified that the present order has been passed keeping in view the
peculiar facts and circumstances of this case, and it shall not be treated as a
precedent in any other case. 
19. As a sequel to the above, the pending interlocutory application, if any,
also stand disposed of. No costs.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

TATA COMMUNICATIONS LTD. & ORS.                  RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Appellant’s service was terminated by his employer. He claimed
reinstatement in service by instituting a suit 1 in the Court of the Civil
Judge, Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. Upon the employer filing an
application under Order VII Rule 11, Code of Civil Procedure, 19082, the
plaint came to be rejected on the ground that Section 14(1)(b) of the
Specific Relief Act, 1963 was a bar to grant of such relief. The
impugned order of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh upheld such
order of rejection of plaint.
2. Having heard Mr. Romy Chacko, learned senior counsel for the
appellant/plaintiff and Mr. Balbir Singh, learned senior counsel for the
respondents/defendants, we are of the view that since a contract of
1  Civil Suit No.205-A/2016
2  CPC
1

--- Page 107 ---
personal service cannot be specifically enforced, the relief of
reinstatement in service could not have been claimed by the appellant;
to that extent, the High Court is right. However, had the appellant
claimed the relief of damages, the suit would be maintainable and the
plaint not liable to rejection. Mr. Chacko submits that since the
application for rejection of plaint came to be allowed, he did not have
the opportunity to seek amendment of the plaint. 
3. Be that as it may, while setting aside the impugned orders of the
trial court and the High Court and reviving the appellant’s suit, we
dispose of the appeal granting liberty to the appellant to seek
amendment of the plaint by filing an application under Order VI Rule
17, CPC within four weeks from date.
4. If the proposed amendment is confined to amending the prayer
clause in the plaint by inserting the relief of damages, instead and in
place of reinstatement, with necessary averments in the body of the
plaint to support a right to claim such relief, the trial court may allow
the prayer for amendment.
5. As and when the application for amendment is allowed, the
defendant(s) shall be granted time to file written statement/additional
written statement.
6. Upon the pleadings being exchanged, the suit shall be taken to
its logical conclusion by the trial court in accordance with law.
7. If no application for amendment is filed by the appellant within
2

--- Page 108 ---
four weeks, this order shall stand recalled and the orders of the trial
court and the High Court restored.
8. The appeal is disposed of on the aforesaid terms, along with
connected interlocutory applications, if any, keeping all points and
contentions on merits open.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

CIVIL APPEAL NO. 14589 OF 2024
SHIV CHARAN DAS                                                   APPELLANT

TATA COMMUNICATIONS LTD. & ORS.                  RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Appellant’s service was terminated by his employer. He claimed
reinstatement in service by instituting a suit 3 in the Court of the Civil
Judge, Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. Upon the employer filing an
application under Order VII Rule 11, Code of Civil Procedure, 19084, the
plaint came to be rejected on the ground that Section 14(1)(b) of the
Specific Relief Act, 1963 was a bar to grant of such relief. The
impugned order of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh upheld such
order of rejection of plaint.
2. Having heard Mr. Romy Chacko, learned senior counsel for the
appellant/plaintiff and Mr. Balbir Singh, learned senior counsel for the
respondents/defendants, we are of the view that since a contract of
personal service cannot be specifically enforced, the relief of
reinstatement in service could not have been claimed by the appellant;
3  Civil Suit No.205-A/2016
4  CPC
6

--- Page 112 ---
to that extent, the trial court and the High Court are right. However,

maintainable and the plaint not liable to rejection. Mr. Chacko submits

did not have the opportunity to seek amendment of the plaint. 
3. Be that as it may, while setting aside the impugned orders of the
trial court and the High Court and reviving the appellant’s suit, we
dispose of the appeal granting liberty to the appellant to seek
amendment of the plaint by filing an application under Order VI Rule
17, CPC within four weeks from date.
4. If the proposed amendment is confined to amending the prayer
clause in the plaint by inserting the relief of damages, instead and in
place of reinstatement, with necessary averments in the body of the
plaint to support a right to claim such relief, the trial court may allow
the prayer for amendment.
5. As and when the application for amendment is allowed, the
defendant(s) shall be granted time to file written statement/additional
written statement.
6. Upon the pleadings being exchanged, the suit shall be taken to
its logical conclusion by the trial court in accordance with law.
7. If no application for amendment is filed by the appellant within
four weeks, this order shall stand recalled and the orders of the trial
court and the High Court restored.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NOs.         OF 2026
(arising out of SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) NOs.33-34/2022)
KAMAL PRABHA BHATT              ...APPELLANT(S)
 
                                VERSUS
DUNGAR SINGH RAWAT DEAD THROUGH LRS. & ORS.   ….RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. We  have  heard  learned  senior  counsel  for  the
appellant and learned senior counsel for the respective
respondent(s) and perused the material on record including
the decree passed by the Trial Court in Suit No.22/84 of
the year 1977-78 by the Court of learned Pargana Officer
and Assistant Collector, First Class, Haldwani, District
Nainital dated 12.04.1979.
3. Admittedly, in the cause title of the said judgment,
the names of the co-defendants, namely, State of Uttar
Pradesh (now State of Uttarakhand) and Gram Sabha were not
typed. Consequently, in the appeal filed by the appellant
herein, who is the judgment debtor, the aforesaid two
authorities were  not arrayed  as parties.  It was  only
1

--- Page 126 ---
thereafter that an application was made under Order 1 Rule
10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (for short, the
CPC) to implead the aforesaid two co-defendants. The said
application was rightly allowed by the appellate court.
4. Being  aggrieved  by  the  said  order,  the
respondent(s)/plaintiff(s)  filed  a  revision  before  the
Additional Commissioner  in which  there was  a stay  of
further proceedings.  The said revision was allowed and
being aggrieved the appellant herein approached the High
Court which  ultimately dismissed  the writ  petition by
impugned order dated 23.11.2020.
5. Learned senior counsel for the appellant submitted
that the suit was filed by the respondent(s)/plaintiff(s)
arraying as many as four defendants.  Admittedly, the
judgment dated 12.04.1979 in the said Suit No.22/84 of the
year 1977-78 did not incorporate the names of two co-
defendants along with the name of appellant herein. The
respondent(s)/plaintiffs(s)  ought  to  have  moved  an
application under Section 152 of the CPC for incorporation
of the names of the two co-defendants before the Trial
Court and thereby seeking correction of the  cause title of
the judgment. The respondent(s)/plaintiff(s) did not take
such a step.  Even the appellant herein did not file any
such application but thereafter moved an application under
2

--- Page 127 ---
Order 41 Rule 20 of the CPC.  The said application though
filed under Order 41 Rule 20 of the CPC was in substance an
application under Section 152 of the CPC for the appellate
forum could also have corrected the said lapse or omission
in the cause title of the judgment of the Trial Court.  The
appellate forum allowed the said application and rightly
so.  Since, it was the respondent(s)/plaintiffs(s) who had
arrayed the said two co-defendants in the Suit.  It was not
a case where for the first time that two new parties were
being impleaded in the appeal.  It was only an omission on
the part of the Trial Court in its judgment which had
omitted to  incorporate names  of two  other defendants,
namely, the State of (Uttar Pradesh) now Uttarakhand and
the  Gram  Sabha  in  the  cause  title  of  the  judgment.
Therefore, the High Court was not right in allowing the
writ petition. In the circumstances, this Court may set
aside the impugned order(s) and restore the order passed by
the appellant forum in the First Appeal so that the appeal
of the appellant could be heard on merits.
6. Per contra , learned senior counsel appearing for the
respective respondent(s)/plaintiff(s) very fairly admitted
that the judgment impugned in the suit did not incorporate
the names of the State of Uttarakhand and the Gram Sabha in
the cause title.  Further, no application was also made  on
3

--- Page 128 ---
behalf of the plaintiffs under Section 152 of the CPC
seeking amendment of the cause title.  Be that as it may.
Learned senior counsel contended that the application for
impleadment was made long thereafter invoking Oder 41 Rule
20 of the CPC and therefore, the said application was hit
by  limitation  and  hence  the  grievance  of  the
respondent(s)/plaintiff(s)  in  that  regard  was  rightly
appreciated by the High Court and there is no merit in
these appeals.
7. We find that this is a case where owing to the
omission on the part of the Trial Court in incorporating
the names of the co-defendants, namely, the State of (Uttar
Pradesh)  now  Uttarakhand  as  well  as  the  Gram  Sabha
ultimately led  to the  application being  filed by  the
appellant herein. The appellate court rightly allowed the
said application.  If the said order allowing the said
application had  not been  assailed by  the respondents,
possibly, long time ago the appeal would have been heard
and disposed of one way or the other.  It is wholly on a
technical plea that the respondent(s)/plaintiff(s) assailed
the order allowing the application for impleadment knowing
fully well that it was not for the first time that those
parties were being impleaded in the appeal by the appellant
herein and it was simply owing to the error which had
4

--- Page 129 ---
occurred in the judgment of the Trial Court which had
omitted to incorporate the names of the said two co-
defendants in the cause title.  
8. In the circumstances, we find that the ends of
justice would be met in the instant case if we set aside
the order(s) of the High Court and restore the order of the
Appellate Court allowing the said application so that the
appeal filed by the appellant herein could be heard on
merits. 
9.  Consequently, we allow these appeals by setting
aside the order(s) of the High Court and restore order
dated 19.10.2004 passed by the Appellate Court/Additional
Commissioner. We direct the said authority to consider the
appeal  filed by the appellant herein on merits after
giving a reasonable opportunity to both sides and after
issuing notice to the State of Uttarakhand and the Gram
Sabha Durgapalpur Parma through its Gram Pradhan .
10. Since the matter is of the year 1977-78 and the
respondents claim that the fruits of the decree have not
yet been fructified, we direct the concerned Commissioner
to dispose of the appeal as early as possible and within a
period of six months once the notices are served on the
State of Uttarakhand and the Gram Sabha Durgapalpur Parma.
5

--- Page 130 ---
 
11. Liberty is also reserved to the appellant herein  to
implead  the  subsequent  purchaser  from  the
respondent(s)/plaintiff(s).
12. Pending disposal of the appeal by the Commissioner,
interim order of status quo regarding possession granted by
this Court on 12.01.2022 shall continue.
13. All pending applications including the application
for intervention/impleadment shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.                             OF 2026
(@SLP(CRL.) NOS.460-461/2025)
ANIL BHALLA & ANR. ETC.  ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF HARYANA & ANR ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Respondent No.2 herein approached the appellants for grant of loan of Rs.3
Lakhs during May, 2021 and they promised to refund the same. Accordingly, a
sum of Rs.2,70,000/- was borrowed and same was not refunded in spite of
repeated requests followed by issuance of legal notice. On account of non-
payment, the appellants are said to have threatened the borrower. Hence, a
complaint came to be lodged which was registered on 05.08.2022 for the
offences punishable under Sections 120B, 403, 406, 420, 384 and 511 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC). Subsequently, a compromise was entered into
between the parties on 20.04.2024 and 20.05.2024, whereunder, all the monies
due to appellants, have been repaid by respondent no. 2 and both parties are
said to have burned their hatchet and did not intent to pursue their grievance.
On account of such settlement having entered into, a petition under Section 482
CrPC was filed by the appellants/petitioners (accused) for quashing of the FIR
and proceedings initiated pursuant to it, which came to be dismissed by the
impugned order. Hence, these appeals.
1

--- Page 149 ---
4. A perusal of the impugned order would indicate that appellants have against
them multiple criminal cases. Taking note of this fact and the allegations that
appellants are charging very high interest and had threatened the complainant
and his family members of dire consequences for non-payment, the High Court
refused to exercise the extra-ordinary jurisdiction to quash the proceedings.
Hence, this appeal.
5. Perusal of the settlement agreement would indicate that appellants and
Respondent No.2 have entered into a settlement and particularly with regard to
the present FIR No. 352 dated 05.08.2022, registered by PS Sector 5,
Panchkula. The learned counsel appearing for respondent-complainant would
also admit that said compromise having been entered into between the parties
and  Respondent No.2 has expressed that he is not inclined to continue the
prosecution. However, learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State
would vehemently oppose the said settlement contending inter  alia that on
account of appellants-accused having been charging high interest which is
contrary to the statutory bar and having posed the threat to Respondent No.2, it
would embolden the appellants to indulge in similar acts. 
6. Having regard to the aforestated facts and also the fact that there has been
a settlement arrived at between the parties without any force, threat or
coercion and the dispute is purely due to the payment of money and there
being no amount now due by the Respondent No.2 payable to the appellants-
accused, continuation of criminal trial would only be a waste of precious judicial
time. As such, the continuation of criminal proceedings would not be warranted.
Hence, the prayer sought for in the appeal stands allowed. The proceedings
pending against the appellants pursuant to FIR No. 352/2022 dated 05.08.2022
on the file of PS Sector 5, Panchkula, and all proceedings thereunder, stands
quashed. No order as to costs.
2

--- Page 150 ---
7. The appeals are allowed accordingly.
8. Pending application(s), if any, stands consigned to records.
..................J.
(ARAVIND KUMAR)

         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIJAY BISHNOI

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard learned counsel for the parties
and have perused the material available on record.
2. The petitioner was terminated from service by
1

--- Page 156 ---
invoking  Rule  6  of  the  Central  Civil  Services
(Temporary  Service)  Rules,  1965  (for  short  ‘1965
Rules’) on the ground that he is physically unfit for
continuance in service. The petitioner questioned the
opinion of the Medical Board. He also invoked the
writ  jurisdiction  of  the  High  Court  seeking  a
direction for a Review Medical Board. The High Court
vide order dated 23.11.2022 directed to hold a Review
Medical Board with a caveat that the petitioner will
not  challenge  the  findings  returned  therein.  The
Review Medical Board found the petitioner not fit for
service  and,  consequently,  the  termination  was
confirmed.
3. Aggrieved therewith, a fresh writ petition was
filed  before  the  High  Court  which  came  to  be
dismissed by the impugned order dated 09.10.2025. The
reliefs  sought  in  the  writ  petition  have  been
summarized in paragraph 1 of the impugned order as
under: 
“(i)  quashing  of  the  termination
letter  dated  13.09.2022  and
consequently,  seeking  re-instatement
to the post of Assistant Commandant
w.e.f. 12.07.2022 with consequential
benefits
2

--- Page 157 ---
(ii) quashing of review medical board
report  dated  17.01.2023  and  the
revised report forwarded vide letter
dated 25.03.2023
(iii)  disburse  salary  of  the
petitioner  for  his  last  month  of
service or alternatively
(iv) re-instate the petitioner to the
post  of  Assistant  Commandant  with
lighter duties as under Circular dated
01.05.2015 and Standing Order No. 4/11
or
(v)  grant  of  ex-gratia  lumpsum
compensation in view of Circular dated
04.08.2017.”
4. The High Court again examined the matter and
found that the Review Medical Board constituted under
the order of the High Court dated 23.11.2022 had
declared  the  petitioner  unfit  for  satisfactory
completion  of  training  or  for  combative  duty  in
future. In consequence, having regard to the previous
undertaking given by the petitioner that he would
abide by the findings of the Review Medical Board
constituted under the order of the High Court dated
23.11.2022, the High Court did not find a good reason
to interfere with the order of termination.
3

--- Page 158 ---
5. Aggrieved by the impugned order, the learned
counsel for the petitioner besides questioning the
findings returned by the Review Medical Board, which
were not open to challenge, has submitted that Rule 6
of the 1965 Rules were not applicable in light of
clause 4(viii) of Circular dated 04.08.2017 which
provided that cases of temporary CRPF personnel /
recruits who are disabled in the performance of bona
fide official  duties  under  various  circumstances,
should not be dealt under CCS (Temporary Service)
Rules, 1965 and that such cases should always be
processed in accordance with the provisions of CCS
(EOP)  Rules,  after  observance  of  all  requisite/
procedural formalities as mentioned in CCS (Medical
Examination) Rules, Standing Order No.04/2011 and CRPF
Medical Manual etc. It is also mentioned therein that
provisions of Rule 6 of the 1965 Rules are relevant
for termination of a temporary government servant
whose  medical  unfitness  is  not  attributable  to
government duty. It is the case of the petitioner that
the  medical  unfitness  was  attributable  to  duty,
therefore, the aforesaid clause was applicable. It is
submitted that the High Court has failed to consider
the matter from that angle. Besides, it has been
4

--- Page 159 ---
urged, the prayer of the petitioner was not limited to
quashing  of  termination,  or  to  quash  the  Review
Medical Board report, there were other prayers also,
such as to reinstate the petitioner to the post of
Assistant Commandant with lighter duties as envisaged
under Circular dated 01.05.2015 and Standing Order
No.04/2011. Additionally, there was an alternative
prayer to grant of ex gratia lump sum compensation in
the  light  of  Circular  dated  04.08.2017.  It  is
submitted that these prayers were also not addressed
by the High Court. 
6. The  learned  counsel  for  the  respondents  has
submitted that those Standing Orders which have been
placed by the petitioner before this Court were not
pressed into service before the High Court as they
were not applicable to a temporary service. Besides,
there was no challenge to the applicability of the
1965 Rules and, in such circumstances, once the Rules
were applicable, the executive instructions, if any,
had to be subservient to the Rules. 
7. We  have  considered  the  submissions  and  have
perused the impugned order.
8. The petitioners have raised various pleas which
do not find mention in the High Court’s order. Whether
5

--- Page 160 ---
those points were urged before the High Court and
inadvertently left out from consideration is an issue
which can be raised before the High Court in a review
petition. Besides, the High Court has not addressed
other prayer(s) made in addition to the prayer seeking
quashing of the termination order and the report of
Review Medical Board. May be those were not pressed.
However, it would not be appropriate on our part to
observe whether those were pressed or not. In case
those points were pressed but not considered by the
High Court, the appropriate course for the petitioner
is to invoke the review jurisdiction of the High
Court.
9. In  such  circumstances,  though  we  affirm  the
finding of the High Court that the petitioner cannot
challenge the opinion of the Review Medical Board,
particularly in light of the undertaking given by the
petitioner in the previous round of litigation, we
deem it appropriate to dispose of this petition by
giving liberty to the petitioner to apply for review
before the High Court, if so advised.
10. In case any such review is filed within 30 days
from today, the same shall be considered in accordance
with law, and it shall not be dismissed as barred by
6

--- Page 161 ---
limitation.
11. With the aforesaid liberty, this special leave
petition is disposed of.
12. We make it clear that the petitioner would have
liberty to challenge the order impugned after decision
on his review, though he would not be allowed to
challenge the findings of the Review Medical Board. 
13. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.                   
  
(CHETAN ARORA)                                  (SAPNA BANSAL)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        COURT MASTER (NSH)
