No.30693/2025)
RATTAN SINGH ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF HARYANA ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant was convicted by the learned Additional
Sessions Judge under Sections 395 and 396 read with
Section 397 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) and
sentenced to undergo various periods of incarceration
including  imprisonment  for  life  for  the  offence
punishable under Section 395 read with Section 397 IPC.
4. Appeal filed by the appellant before the High Court
of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh (briefly the ‘High
Court’ hereinafter) was rejected vide the judgment and
order dated 08.11.2011.
5. On 27.07.2026, we had issued notice on the question
of permanent remission as well as on the application for
1

--- Page 170 ---
condonation of delay.
6. As noticed supra, today we have condoned the delay.
7. From  the  custody  certificate,  it  is  seen  that
appellant  has  undergone  actual  imprisonment  without
remission for about 22 years and with remission it would
be about 25 years.
8. This Court, in the case of In Re: Policy Strategy
for Grant of Bail [2025 SCC OnLine SC 349],  recorded
the following conclusions:
“21.  We,  therefore,  record  the  following
conclusions:
a) Where  there  is  a  policy  of  the
appropriate Government laying down guidelines
for consideration of the grant of premature
release under Section 432 of the CrPC or
Section 473 of the BNSS, it is the obligation
of the appropriate Government to consider
cases of all convicts for grant of premature
release as and when they become eligible for
consideration in terms of the policy. In such
a case, it is not necessary for the convict
or  his  relatives  to  make  a  specific
application for grant of permanent remission.
When  the  jail  manual  or  any  other
departmental  instruction  issued  by  the
appropriate Government contains such policy
guidelines,  the  aforesaid  direction  will
apply;
b) We  direct  those  States  and  Union
Territories that do not have a policy dealing
with the grant of remission in terms of
Section 432 of the CrPC or Section 473 of the
BNSS to formulate a policy within two months
from today;
2

--- Page 171 ---
c) Appropriate Government has the power to
incorporate suitable conditions in an order
granting permanent remission. Consideration
of various factors, which are mentioned in
paragraph 13 above by way of illustration, is
necessary before finalizing the conditions.
The conditions must aim at ensuring that the
criminal tendencies, if any, of the convict
remain  in  check  and  that  the  convict
rehabilitates himself in the society. The
conditions should not be so oppressive or
stringent that the convict is not able to
take  advantage  of  the  order  granting
permanent remission. The conditions cannot be
vague  and  should  be  capable  of  being
performed;
d) Order granting or refusing the relief of
permanent  remission  must  contain  brief
reasons. The order containing reasons should
be immediately communicated to the convict
through the office of the concerned prison.
The copies thereof should be forwarded to the
Secretaries of the concerned District Legal
Services Authorities. It is the duty of the
prison authorities to inform the convict that
he has the right to challenge the order of
rejection of the prayer for the grant of
remission.
e) As held in the case of Mafabhai Motibhai
Sagar, an order granting permanent remission
cannot  be  withdrawn  or  cancelled  without
giving an opportunity of being heard to the
convict.  An  order  of  cancellation  of
permanent  remission  must  contain  brief
reasons;
f) The District Legal Services Authorities
shall endeavour to implement NALSA SOP in its
true letter and spirit.
g) Further,  the  District  Legal  Services
3

--- Page 172 ---
Authorities shall also monitor implementation
of conclusion (a) as recorded above. For this
purpose,  the  District  Legal  Services
Authorities shall maintain the relevant date
of the convicts and as and when they become
eligible to a consideration for grant of
premature release, they shall do the needful
in terms of conclusion (a). The State Legal
Services  Authorities  shall  endeavour  to
create  a  portal  on  which  the  data  as
aforesaid  can  be  uploaded  on  real  time
basis.”
9. In terms of Paragraph 21(g) of the conclusions
extracted  herein  above,  District  Legal  Services
Authorities  have  been  mandated  to  monitor
implementation of conclusion (a). For this purpose,
the  District  Legal  Services  Authorities  shall
maintain the relevant data of the convicts and as and
when they become eligible for a consideration for
grant of premature release, they shall do the needful
in terms of conclusion (a). The State Legal Services
Authorities shall endeavour to create a portal on
which the data as aforesaid can be uploaded on real
time basis.
10. We, therefore, direct the appropriate Government,
i.e. State of Haryana, to consider the case for
permanent remission of the appellant as per the
applicable remission policy.
11. The District Legal Services Authority of Sonipat
shall do the needful so that the remission papers of
4

--- Page 173 ---
the  appellant can  be  transmitted  to  the  State
Government for necessary consideration.
12. In  view  of  the  long  incarceration  of  the
appellant, we direct, as an interim measure, that the
appellant shall be released on bail from custody on
his Personal Bond.
13. Interim bail granted to the appellant shall not
be taken as a factor against the appellant while
considering his case for permanent remission.
14. Let the consideration be carried out within three
months from today.
15. List thereafter on 13.01.2027.

--- Page 208 ---
- 2 -
2. This Special Leave Petition is filed by the petitioner, who is
an auction-purchaser against order dated 29.04.2025 by which in
the writ petition filed by the borrower, it has been held that
right  of  redemption  is  available  to  the  borrower  despite
issuance of sale certificate and execution of the sale deed. The
High Court noted that the borrower has deposited a sum of Rs.
14,00,000/- (Rupees Fourteen Lakhs only) with the banks to show
his bona fides on 06.06.2025. Accordingly, the writ petition was
allowed.
3. Admittedly, the borrower is in possession of the property in
question. During the pendency of this Special Leave Petition,
the parties arrived at some kind of a settlement. It has been
stated before us that the petitioner would be satisfied if a sum
of Rs. 20,00,000/- (Rupees Twenty Lakhs only) is paid to him.
4. The petitioner had deposited a sum of Rs. 13.65 Lakhs as sale
consideration with the bank. The said amount shall be returned
to the petitioner by the bank.
5. In addition, the respondent-borrower shall refund a sum of Rs.
6.35 Lakhs to the petitioner within a period of four months
from today. 
6. The respondent-borrower had deposited a sum of Rs. 14,00,000/-
(Rupees Fourteen Lakhs only) with the banks on 06.06.2025.

--- Page 209 ---
Therefore, the bank shall refund the interest accrued on  the
aforesaid amount at the rate of 6% per annum to the respondent-
borrower.
Contd..
 - 3 -
7. Accordingly, the Special Leave Petition stands disposed of.
8. Pending interlocutory application(s), if any, is/are disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Criminal) No. 11602 of 2026)

1. Leave granted.
2. The  present  petition  has  been  filed  for
cancellation of bail granted to the respondent No. 2 vide
order dated 11.09.2025 passed by the High Court of
Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow in Criminal Appeal No.
3768 of 2024.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner, while arguing
the matter for cancellation of bail, has drawn the
attention of this Court to the medico-legal report/post-
mortem report, pointing out that there are as many as
eight ante-mortem injuries found on the body of the
deceased. Attention has also been invited to the fact
that the post-mortem report reveals that the deceased was
1

--- Page 225 ---
one month pregnant at the time of death.
4. Learned  counsel  appearing  on  behalf  of  the
respondent No. 1-State of Uttar Pradesh has supported the
petition and has prayed for cancellation of bail, relying
upon the findings recorded in the post-mortem report.
5. On the other hand, learned counsel for respondent
No. 2 has submitted that after the deceased was found
hanging, the husband brought her body down and carried
her to the hospital, and in that process, the deceased
might have sustained the injuries that find mention in
the medico-legal report.
6. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and
upon perusal of the record, including the medico-legal
report and post-mortem report, this Court is of the
opinion that the application for cancellation of bail
deserves to be allowed and is accordingly allowed. 
7. The impugned order dated 11.09.2025 passed by the
High Court is set aside.
8. The bail granted to the respondent No. 2 stands
cancelled. Respondent No. 2 is granted four weeks’ time
to surrender before the competent court.
9. The Trial Court is directed to conclude the trial
as expeditiously as possible, preferably within a period
of one year from today.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S). 8532/2019
M/S MALAYAGIRI SANDALWOOD OIL DISTILLERY APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF U.P. AND ORS.     RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The present appeal arises out of an order dated
31.08.2015 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad, Lucknow Bench at Lucknow in Misc. Bench No.
2538 of 2011, whereby the High Court declined to
interfere  in  the  matter  and  dismissed  the  Writ
Petition preferred by the appellant.
2. The facts of the case reveal that an auction
notice  was  issued  for  the  sale/disposal  of  red
sanders/sandalwood  by  the  Divisional  Sale  Manager,
Uttar  Pradesh  Forest  Corporation,  Lucknow  on
24.12.2010. The appellant participated in the auction
process  upon  depositing  a  sum  of  Rs.  2,00,000/-
(Rupees Two Lakh only) and quoted a rate of Rs. 360/-
per kilogram.
3. Subsequent to the auction, multiple complaints
were received in the matter. Consequently, by an order
1

--- Page 230 ---
dated  01.02.2011,  the  respondent(s)  cancelled  the
auction process.
4. Being  aggrieved  by  the  cancellation,  the
appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court.
The High Court dismissed the writ petition, reserving
liberty to the appellant to either take recourse to
the arbitration or seek remedies by instituting a
civil suit for breach of contract. Challenging the
said decision, the appellant has preferred the present
appeal.
5. This Court has carefully perused the record and
the reply filed on behalf of the respondent(s). The
reply reveals that following the auction, complaints
were  lodged  before  the  authorities,  stating  that
several prospective bidders who were willing to offer
higher rate of Rs. 600/- per kilogram were prevented
from participating in the auction by the local mafia.
In  view  of  these  circumstances,  the  competent
authority took a conscious policy decision to cancel
the auction.
6. Under  these  facts,  the  High  Court  rightly
declined  to  exercise  its  discretionary  writ
jurisdiction and granted liberty to seek recourse to
the arbitration or seek remedies by instituting a
civil suit for breach of contract.
2

--- Page 231 ---
7. Considering that the auction pertains to the
year 2010 and almost 16 years have elapsed since then,
this Court does not find any ground to interfere with
the order dated 01.02.2011 by which the auction was
cancelled in the peculiar facts and circumstances of
the case.
8. However, it is directed that if the earnest
money/security deposit of the appellant has not been
refunded so far, the respondent(s) shall refund the
entire  deposited  amount  to  the  appellant,  with
interest at the rate of 12% per annum, within a period
of sixty days from today.
9. With  the  aforesaid  observations,  the  appeal
stands disposed of.
10. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.
 ………………………………………………………J.
[SATISH CHANDRA SHARMA]
   
………………………………………………………J.
[NONGMEIKAPAM KOTISWAR SINGH]
NEW DELHI;

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S). 1255/2016
THE STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
PREM PAL & ANR.     RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The present appeal arises out of the judgment dated
19.02.2016 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad in Criminal Appeal No. 1294 of 1997, whereby the
High Court allowed the appeal preferred by the accused
persons/respondent(s) and set aside their conviction and
sentence. 
2. The  facts  of  the  case  reveal  that  the  First
Information Report was lodged by Chhangey Lal, stating that
he and his son were sent to District Jail, Bareilly, from
Police Station Faridpur on 03.02.1990. While inside the
jail, the accused persons, namely, Prem Pal and Narottam,
who were Constables, allegedly demanded a bribe and, upon
non-fulfilment of the said demand, subjected the victims to
torture, abuse, and physical assault. On account of the
injuries sustained by them, they were initially sent to the
Jail Hospital and subsequently shifted to the District
1

--- Page 235 ---
Hospital.  The  condition  of  the  informant's  son
deteriorated, and he ultimately succumbed to his injuries
on 24.02.1990 at the District Hospital. The injuries were
allegedly caused by the assault committed inside the jail
by Prem Pal, Narottam, and two others, namely, Rishipal and
Chuttiman.
3. Following investigation by the police, charge-sheet
was  filed,  and  it  was  found  that  there  were  several
injuries on the body of the deceased. During the trial, as
many as twenty-two (22) prosecution witnesses and two (02)
defence witnesses were examined. The Trial Court convicted
the accused persons for offences punishable under Section
304 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and Section 3(2)(vii)
of  the  Scheduled  Castes  and  the  Scheduled  Tribes
(Prevention  of  Atrocities)  Act,  1989,  and  awarded  a
sentence of ten years' rigorous imprisonment along with a
fine of Rs. 10,000/-. Being aggrieved, the accused persons
preferred Criminal Appeal No. 1294 of 1997 before the High
Court of Judicature at Allahabad.
4. The High Court, upon a meticulous scanning of the
evidence on record, allowed the appeal and acquitted the
accused persons.
5. This Court has carefully gone through the entire
record.  It  is  an  admitted  fact  that  the  injured  was
admitted to the District Hospital and, even according to
the prosecution's own case, there was no allegation of any
2

--- Page 236 ---
assault on the informant or his son prior to 09.02.1990.
The alleged occurrence inside the jail took place on
11.02.1990.
6. Perusal of the testimonies of the witnesses reveals
that the material prosecution witnesses, namely, PW-1, PW-
2, and PW-3, turned hostile and failed to support the case
of the prosecution. Furthermore, the dying declaration of
the deceased, recorded on 12.02.1990 at 6:15 p.m. by the
Deputy  Collector,  Bareilly,  contained  specific  and
categorical allegations against police officers of Police
Station Baradari, specifically naming Constable Nathua,
Constable Pandey, and three Inspectors. Neither of the
respondents,  Prem  Pal  or  Narottam,  was  named  by  the
deceased in the said dying declaration, nor was any action
taken against the police personnel who were actually named
therein.
7. The High Court, relying upon the dying declaration
recorded  on  12.02.1990  at  6:15  p.m.  by  the  Deputy
Collector, Bareilly, and noting that the accused persons
were  not  named  therein,  set  aside  the  judgment  of
conviction and order of sentence dated 03.06.1997 passed by
the II Additional Sessions Judge, Bareilly, in Sessions
Trial No. 302 of 1995, titled "State vs. Prem Pal and
Another", arising out of Case Crime No. 229 of 1990, Police
Station Kotwali, District Bareilly.
8. In the present appeal, it has been brought on record
3

--- Page 237 ---
that respondent No. 1, Prem Pal, has expired, leaving
respondent  No.  2,  Narottam,  as  the  sole  surviving
respondent.
9. Having regard to the evidence on record, this Court
finds no cogent ground or justification to take a view
different from that arrived at by the High Court.
10. The appeal is, accordingly, dismissed.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.           /2026
@ SLP (CRIMINAL) No(s). 9697/2026
HARDEEP SINGH & ANR.                            Appellant (s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF HARYANA & ANR.                         Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. Heard learned Counsel for
the appellants and the respondent-State. 
2. Despite service of notice on the second
respondent, as is reported by the office vide
Office Report dated 23.09.2026, no one has
entered appearance on her behalf.
3. The appellants were made accused by a
First  Information  Report  (for  short  ‘FIR’)
dated  06.01.2022  lodged  by  the  second
respondent at Women Police Station, District
Kurukshetra, Haryana for offences punishable
under Sections 323, 406, 498-A and 506 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short ‘IPC’). The
FIR was investigated and a police report was
submitted  based  on  which  proceedings  were
initiated  and  charges  were  framed.  The
1

--- Page 240 ---
appellants  applied  for  quashing  of  the
proceedings by invoking the inherent powers of
the High Court based on a compromise dated
29.11.2024 which indicated that the allegations
were in the context of matrimonial disputes
between the parties which have been settled by
mutual consent as also a mutual divorce where
under alimony etc. was paid by the husband to
the respondent.
4. There  was  no  dispute  regarding  such
settlement  having  been  arrived  at  between
parties. However, the High Court declined the
prayer to quash the proceedings on the ground
that the first appellant (Hardeep Singh) i.e.
the husband had obtained bail in connection
with the present case but had jumped the bail
by not appearing before the court and was
declared a proclaimed absconder. The High Court
took the view that since the first appellant
had misused the concession of bail and had left
the  country,  he  was  not  entitled  to  the
discretionary relief available to him under the
inherent powers of the High Court.
5. The  submission  on  behalf  of  the
2

--- Page 241 ---
appellants is that there is no dispute that
parties have settled their differences and have
obtained divorce by mutual consent. In such
circumstances,  having  already  applied  for
quashing of the proceedings, if he had left for
Canada  being  employed  there,  there  was  no
justification to deny him relief. It has also
been submitted that the law is settled that
where  criminal  proceedings  emanate  from
matrimonial disputes and parties resolve their
differences  and  pray  for  quashing  of  the
proceedings  based  on  a  compromise,  those
proceedings  even  if  they  relate  to  non
compoundable offences can be quashed under the
inherent powers of the High Court1.
6. The learned counsel for the respondent-
State has submitted that the State has no
objection if the parties have already resolved
their  differences  and  have  entered  into  a
settlement.
7. Having regard to the facts of the case
and  the  submissions  made  before  us,  while
taking into account that there is a settlement
between parties and despite service of notice,
1  B.S Joshi vs. State of Haryana and Anr.: (2003) 4 SCC 675 
3

--- Page 242 ---
the  second  respondent  has  not  entered  an
appearance to refute the settlement which has
been annexed with the appeal paperbook, we are
of the view that the proceedings are liable to
be quashed on the basis of mutual settlement
between  the  parties  more  so  when  those
proceedings  have  emanated  from  matrimonial
differences.
8. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The
order of the High Court dated 13.03.2026 is set
aside. The criminal proceedings emanating from
FIR  No.  3/2022  at  Women  Police  Station,
District  Kurukshetra,  Haryana  and  all
consequential proceedings are hereby quashed.
9. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall
stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The original applicants who had filed the application
before the Central Administrative Tribunal (for short
‘CAT’)  were  from  the  unreserved  category.  Their
1

--- Page 245 ---
grievance was that candidates who had participated in
the recruitment exercise under the reserved category
had  migrated  to  the  unreserved  category  thereby
depriving the candidates from the unreserved category
of their right to be considered for appointment against
unreserved seats/posts.
2. Migration of a candidate from reserved category to the
unreserved category may not be permissible where the
candidate has taken benefit of any kind of relaxation
available to that reserved category.
3. However, here, it is not clear from the orders of the
CAT  as  well  as  the  High  Court  whether  any  such
relaxation was availed by candidates belonging to the
reserved  category  who  migrated  to  the  unreserved
category at the stage of final selection. 
4. What appears from the order of the CAT is that the
examination was in two stages. The first stage was
Computer Based Test referred to as CBT and the second
stage was Computer Based Aptitude Test referred to as
CBAT.  CAT in paragraph 13 of its order records a
2

--- Page 246 ---
finding in the following terms:
“...In the instant case, the respondents
have switched the category of candidates in
exam to exam (CBT to CBAT) to give undue
benefit to the candidates of their own
choice  by  giving  relaxation  from  their
particular community.”  
5. It is, however, not clear from the orders of the CAT as
well as the High Court as to whether a separate cut-off
for qualifying CBT was specified category wise; and
whether the cut-off for CBT was lower for the reserved
category than what it was for the unreserved category;
and whether the candidates from the reserved category
who got empaneled in the final select list against
unreserved seats/ posts had availed the benefit of that
lower cut-off. 
6. To have clarity on the issue, we deem it appropriate to
require the petitioner to file an additional affidavit
explaining the following:
(i) Whether  the  candidates  who  had
applied under the reserved category
and  were  empaneled  in  the  final
select  list  against  unreserved
3

--- Page 247 ---
seats/posts had taken benefit of any
kind  of  relaxation  in  the
recruitment  process  available  to
that  category.  If  any  such
relaxation was provided to them, the
nature of such relaxation shall be
disclosed; and
(ii)Whether  for  participation  in  the
CBAT test a candidate was required
to have marks above a specified cut-
off in the CBT test. Whether such
cut off varied category wise. If so,
whether  the  candidates  from  the
reserved  category,  placed  in  the
final select list against unreserved
posts/seats,  had  obtained  marks
higher than the cut-off fixed for
the unreserved category in the CBT
test.
7. Let aforesaid details be provided in the affidavit for
which four weeks’ time is allowed. 
4

--- Page 248 ---
8. List on 27.10.2026.
SLP (C) No. 11296/2026

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
(Arising out of S.L.P. (Crl) No. 17286 of 2025)
NITIN GARG  ...APPELLANT
VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ANR.     ...RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard the learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the appellant and the learned A.S.G. appearing for the
respondents.
3. The appellant before us is aggrieved by the order
passed by the High Court of Delhi by which, the Lookout
Circular issued against him by respondent No.1 was not
interfered with.
4. The  learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant submitted that on few of the previous occasions,
the appellant has travelled abroad. He has been travelling
abroad due to his professional commitments by visiting
referral firms and that is why he has been frequently
visiting three countries primarily.
5. Considering the above, it is submitted that there is
1

--- Page 255 ---
no  need  for  a  Lookout  Circular,  especially  when  the
appellant is a Chartered Accountant with whom around two
hundred associates are working.  He is not a flight risk,
as he has always cooperated with the investigation and
inquiry.
6. The learned A.S.G. appearing for the respondents
submitted that there exists a suspicion in the appellant
frequently travelling abroad.  There is no need for him to
travel abroad. Furthermore, the High Court has rejected
the  quashing  application  only  on  the  question  of
jurisdiction.  
7. Having heard the parties, we make it clear that we do
not wish to stand on technicalities.  Suffice it to state
that the Lookout Circular against the appellant, who is a
Chartered Accountant having his own firm, is not required,
as he is not a flight risk. 
8. In such view of the matter, we set aside the Lookout
Circular issued against the appellant by the respondent
No.1 with a direction to the appellant that he shall
inform the concerned respondent(s) fifteen days prior to
each of his visits abroad in the future, by giving the
itinerary and the details of the places he intends to
visit to the concerned respondent(s). 
2

--- Page 256 ---
9. Accordingly, the appeal stands allowed in the above
terms. 
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.           /2026
(@ SLP(C) No. 21666/2026)
SRS BUILDING MATERIAL SUPPLIER ..... APPELLANT(S)
            VERSUS
M/S S.B. ASSOCIATES ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
 
1. Leave granted. 
2. Though the High Court, by way of the impugned order dated
10.04.2026, opined that there was no arbitration agreement
between  the  parties  and  refused  to  exercise  power  and
jurisdiction to appoint an Arbitrator under Section 11 of the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 1, we find that the
arbitration clause in the present case reads as under:-
“Any dispute or difference between the parties
arising out of or touching upon the conditions
covered under this agreement may be settled
amicable  by  the  Managing  Director
/Partner/Proprietor of Party-A and Party-B. in
the event of disagreement, they may refer such
1  For short ‘1996 Act’

--- Page 301 ---
dispute/differences  Sole  Arbitrator  if  the
parties in dispute so agree, other wise on
arbitrator nominated by each of the Party. In
the case of defences of opinion between them the
decision of the umpire selected by them and the
proceedings conducted as per Arbitration and
Conciliation and binding on both the parties.
However, the progress of the work will not be
affected during arbitral proceedings or dispute
resolving period.”
3. We are of the opinion that the High Court was not justified in
inferring an element of choice as to whether or not to
arbitrate as such choice seems to have been contemplated only
in the context of either deciding upon a sole Arbitrator or in
the event of failure in that regard, each party nominating a
separate Arbitrator to represent it.
4. The appeal is allowed, setting aside the impugned order passed
the by High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh. In
consequence and keeping in mind the quantum of the claim
raised by the appellant, which would be the subject matter of
the arbitration proceedings, we appoint Ms. Kamini Lau, former
District Judge, Delhi Higher Judicial Service , Delhi, to act
as the sole Arbitrator to resolve the disputes inter  se the
parties. 
5. The learned Arbitrator shall file her declaration/disclosure,
in terms of Section 12 of the 1996 Act, within a period of
fifteen days from the date a copy of this order is received by
her.  She shall be entitled to the fees prescribed under the
Fourth Schedule to the 1996 Act. 

--- Page 302 ---
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of

(SANJAY KUMAR)
.....................J.
(SANJEEV SACHDEVA)
NEW DELHI;
SEPTEMBER 24, 2026.

1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant has been arraigned as an accused
and seeks regular bail in connection with FIR
No.RC-01/2023/NIA/AMD  dated  01.07.2023,
registered with NIA Police Station Ahmedabad,
for the offences punishable under Sections 38
and 39 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention)
Act, 1967 and Section 120-B of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860.
3. We  have  heard  the  learned  Senior  counsel
appearing for the appellant as well as the
learned Additional Solicitor General and the
learned counsel appearing for the respondents.
4. Pursuant to the earlier order, the main witness
has been examined and additionally one more
1  SLP(Crl.) No.4230/2026

--- Page 325 ---
witness is being examined today. 
5. We also take note of the fact that apart from
the  period  of  incarceration,  the  appellant
before us is a lady having two minor children
and,  therefore,  differential  treatment  is
required, particularly, in the light of the
scheme  under  the  Bhartiya  Nagarik  Suraksha
Sanhita, 2023.
6. Considering the above, we are inclined to set
aside the impugned order passed by the High
Court, and grant regular bail to the appellant.
7. Accordingly,  the  impugned  order  stands  set
aside, and the appellant is granted regular
bail, subject to the terms and conditions that
may be imposed by the concerned Trial Court.
8. The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.
9. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

                   Mr. Abhay Singh Yadav, Adv.
                  For M/s Lex Regis Law Offices, AOR               
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Paras 14 and 15 respectively of the impugned Order passed by
the High Court read thus:-
“14. The nature of the suit is of material significance.
The instant suits are for specific performance of the
contract. The presence of the Petitioner is not at all
necessary to adjudicate the controversy that arises in a
suit for specific performance of the contract for sale. The
Petitioner is not claiming through the Defendant, either.
The Petitioner asserts that the Petitioner has the right
develop the suit property on the basis of the development
agreements purportedly executed by the societies of slum
dwellers. The Petitioner has, thus, no direct interest in
the subject matter of the suit for specific performance.
15. The Petitioner could, undoubtedly, agitate its rights
as a new developer over the suit property in an appropriate
proceedings before the appropriate forum. However, the
Petitioner cannot seek impleadment in the instant suits on
the premise that the acknowledgment of possession, or for
that  matter  the  passing  of  the  decree  for  specific
performance, would jeopardise the rights of the Petitioner.
In substance, there is neither privity of contract nor
identity of the dispute, between the original parties to
the suit and the Petitioner.”
2. Having heard the learned Senior counsel appearing for the
parties and having gone through the materials on record, we are of
the view that we should not interfere with the common impugned
Orders passed by the High Court.
3. If the petitioner has any independent right to enforce insofar
as the property in question is concerned, it shall be open for it
to avail appropriate legal remedy before the appropriate forum in
accordance with law.
4. All contentions in law are kept open for the parties to raise
before the appropriate forum.
5. With the aforesaid, these petitions stand disposed of.

3

1. The  present  petitions  arise  out  of  the  common
impugned order dated 08.06.2026 passed by the High Court of
Judicature at Bombay in Writ Petition Nos. 5994 and 6668 of
2025.
2. The facts of the case reveal that a crime case was
registered at Police Station N.M. Joshi Marg, for the
1

--- Page 399 ---
offences punishable under Sections 318(4) and 61 of the BNS1
and Sections 3, 4 and 13 of the MOFA2.
3. It is further revealed from the record that an
amount of Rs. 1,89,48,000/- was recovered from the accused
persons, which the Trial Court directed to be released in
favour of the complainant on superdari. Aggrieved thereby,
the writ petition No. 5994 of 2025 was preferred before the
High Court, whereby the High Court, after hearing the
parties at length, modified the direction and ordered that
the recovered amount be invested in an interest bearing
fixed deposit account with the Court.
4. In the considered opinion of this Court, at a pre-
trial stage, the release of the seized amount in favour of
the first informant was certainly not proper, and the High
Court was fully justified in directing the deposit of the
money in an interest-bearing fixed deposit account.
5. Consequently, we do not find any reason to interfere
with the impugned order passed by the High Court. However,
we request the Trial Court to expedite the trial and
conclude the same as expeditiously as possible, preferably
within a period of one year from today. It is further made
clear that the Trial Court shall not grant any unnecessary
adjournments in the matter.

1. Leave granted.

‘IPC’) and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life
with fine.
4. Appeal filed by the appellant before the High Court
of Chhattisgarh (briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter)
assailing  his  aforesaid  conviction  and  sentence  was
partly allowed by the High Court  vide  the impugned
judgment and order dated 04.04.2024. The conviction and

sentence of the appellant under Section 302 of the IPC

that the deceased was in an intoxicated State and it was
he who was abusing the appellant and others. Unable to
control himself, appellant assaulted the deceased with
his hands and fists.

appellant should be enlarged on bail during the pendency
of the criminal appeal before this Court.
8. Accordingly, it is directed that the appellant shall

conditions.

Court has committed an error in holding that prior approval of
the State is mandated before the appellant can initiate
investigation, notwithstanding, the fact that the registration

by the High Court. Incidentally, the facts have been gone into
which was not required at that stage.

application to be filed. The appearance of the respondents is
dispensed with until and unless the same is required by the
concerned Court.

appeal stands allowed, accordingly.

For Petitioner(s) : Mr. Vinay Garg, AOR (through VC)
                   
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. It is argued that the respondent
joined the service on 10.06.1982 as a daily
wager and at the time of regularization in
the  year  2006,  respondent  submitted  an
affidavit and filled Form ‘A’ showing his
date of birth as 01.05.1962. In the year
2015, the respondent applied for change in
the date of birth on the basis of a school

--- Page 1022 ---
2
leaving certificate showing his date of birth
as 01.07.1968, which was coincidentally the
date of birth recorded in the EPF record.
Subsequently, the respondent preferred a writ
petition in the year 2020 seeking change of
date of birth in the service record.
2. Learned counsel for the petitioner
would submit that if the petitioner’s date of
birth  is  taken  as  01.07.1968  then,  the
respondent would be only 14 years of age at
the time when he joined the service as a
daily wager, which is impermissible.
3. Issue  notice,  returnable  on
29.10.2026.
4. In the meanwhile, there shall be
stay on the impugned order passed by the High
Court.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
As per the Office report, unregistered SLP has already been
withdrawn  vide  the  Hon'ble  Judge-in-Chamber's  order  dated
